newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries crawl up in London but jitters dominate.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries crawl up in London but jitters dominate.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries crawled up from their overnight lows in London, but the market remained jittery after fresh data signalling stronger-than-expected economic growth, traders said on Thursday.

A sharp drop in the March U.S. trade gap on Wednesday hammered the long end of the U.S. yield curve, fuelling expectations of a rate hike in July after the Federal Reserve's decision to hold fire on Tuesday.
But the short end managed cling to earlier gains.
"The long end of the curve is quite vulnerable," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London.
"After the sharp fall yesterday, we may get a slight rebound but market sentiment is pretty negative," he added.
By 1030 GMT, the 30-year T-bond was at 95-26 yielding 6.96 percent, up from 95-24 in Tokyo and unchanged from New York. The two-year note was at 100-08, unchanged from both overnight levels.
Traders said the Fed's inaction on Tuesday and the subsequent strong economic data triggered concerns that the Fed could lag behind the yield curve.
"Just as the Fed was preemptive in March, it should have been preemptive in May," Stamenkovic said. "The market is concerned about any potential inflation rise."
A trader at French bank in London said unless the next set of data confirmed the Fed was right to leave rates unchanged, further losses in the long end would be inevitable.
"The market is agnostic about it and waiting to see the next set of data," he said.
"If you were to get more troublesome data indicating that the economy is picking up again...the yield curve will start to steepen again," he said.
The two-year note to 30-year bond spread was at 73 basis points by 1030 GMT, up three from Wednesday's midday levels.
"We should still get good inflation news so the downside to the market may be somewhat limited," said Stamenkovic.
The weekly jobless claims expected at 1230 GMT should have little impact on Treasuries on Thursday unless they show a sharp fall, traders said.
The focus however is shifting towards the May U.S. payrolls data expected on June 6 for fresh clues on economic recovery.
In the meantime, speculation about a rate hike in Japan could also prompt some selling on the front-end of the U.S. curve by Japanese investors, traders said.
By 1030 GMT, the June T-bond future was at 109-08 compared with the Chicago close of 109-09.
